docs.title: work on someone else's code
docs.text:
When work on someone else's repo (original repo), push only to our own repo, and pull updates from the original repo.

  • origin = your private repo (push here)
  • upstream = original repo (pull only)

docs.title: One‑time Setup:
docs.text:
# 1) Clone the original repo (example GIOS course project 1)
git clone https://github.gatech.edu/gios-spr-26/pr1.git
cd pr1

# 2) Point origin to your repo
git remote set-url origin https://github.gatech.edu/<gtid>/gios-spr-26-pr1.git

# 3) Add the original repo as upstream (read‑only)
git remote add upstream https://github.gatech.edu/gios-spr-26/pr1.git

# 4) Disable pushing to upstream (safety)
git remote set-url --push upstream PUSH_DISABLED

# 5) Verify
git remote -v

docs.title: Later Workflow (sync update + develop)
docs.text:
# Optional: If you have local uncommitted changes before pulling
git stash -u

# Get updates from original repo when needed
git checkout main
git pull --rebase upstream main
# Optional: keep your private repo's main in sync too
git push origin main

# Optional: If you have local uncommitted changes and ran git stash -u before
git stash pop

# Work on your code
# Create a new feature branch (Don’t develop directly on main!). Use -b only once for first creation
git checkout -b my-feature

# Push your feature branch to your private repo
git push -u origin my-feature

Then next time on same feature branch: 

git checkout my-feature
git pull --rebase
git push

docs.text:
solve computation problems, and communicate that our solutions are correct and efficient.

Term Definition Requirements Example Define Problem A mapping (binary relation) from problem inputs to correct outputs. • Usually don’t specify every correct output for all inputs (too many examples; one input could map to many output) • Provide a verifiable predicate (a property) that correct outputs must satisfy (so we can check whether the output is correct or not given a input-output pair) • general problem, arbitrarily large input size** • Not general: small input instance: In this room, is there a pair of students with same birthday? • General: arbitrarily large inputs: Given any set of n students, is there a pair of students with same birthday? (include year, date, hour, etc.) Design Algorithms a sequence of procedure to map each input to a single correct output (like a function) to solve birthday matching: – Maintain a record of names and birthdays (initially empty) – Interview each student in some order * If birthday exists in record, return found pair! * Else add name and birthday to record – Return None if last student interviewed without success Prove Correctness • For small inputs, can use case analysis • For arbitrarily large inputs, algorithm must be recursive or loop in some way • Must use induction ( recursion is such a key concept in computer science) • Example: Proof of correctness of birthday matching algorithm

docs.title: What is an Operating System?
docs.text: Item Definition higher level Applications - laptop/desktop/phone: browser, editor, messaging, music apps etc  - datacenter: web server, database, simulation Operating System (OS) Software layer between apps and hardware to abstract complex hardware and manage hardware resources (arbitration).  Elements:  file system, device driver, CPU scheduler etc  Visual metaphor: shop manager (allocates resources, schedules work, enforces rules). Hardware - Central Processing Units (CPUs)  - Physical Memory  - Network Interconnects (Ethernet port/Wifi Card)  - Graphic Processing Units (GPU)  - Storage Devices (hard Disk, SSDs, Flash drives [USB]) ---- Figure: OS sits between apps and hardware

docs.title: Main functions of OS
docs.text:
Function What it means Quick example Hide hardware complexity Directly has privileged access to the underlying hardware and provide simpler abstractions than raw devices to apps - Support different types of devices - File abstraction instead of a block of disk storage: read/write - Internet Socket abstraction instead of bits and packets: send/receive Allocate, Manage resources Manages hardware on behalf of applications according to some predefined policies. Decide how many and which resources will the app use, e.g., CPU, memory, IO - allocates memory for applications - schedules apps for execution on the CPU -controls access to various devices and so on Isolation & protection Ensures that applications are isolated and prevent concurrent apps from harming each other - Allocate each apps different parts of underlying phycial memory - Make sure one application can’t read/write another’s memory ---

Examples of OS | Category| Examples | |---|---| | Desktop | - Microsoft Windows - Unix-based : Mac OS X (extend BCD), Linux| | Embedded | Android, iOS, Symbian | | Server||

docs.text:
Term Meaning Examples Abstraction “What” interface you program against - For applications: Process/thread; - For hardware: file (storage), socket (network card), memory page (phycial memory) Mechanism “How” the OS performs operations on abstractions - Create/schedule process/thread to run on CPU; - open/read/write/allocate hardware resources Policy "How"he mechanisms will be used to manage the underlying hardware - The max number of sockets an application can access - Which data can be removed from memory: - Page replacement: Least-recently used (LRU) / earliest deadline first (EDF) ----

Example memory management: | Component | In memory management | |---|---| | Abstraction | Memory page (fixed-size addressable region) of memory| | Mechanisms | - Allocate page in DRAM - map the memory page into a process addres to allow the process access the actual physical memory - move pages from DRAM to disk accorrding to polices (swapping). | | Policy | The Least recently used (LRU) (unimportant, likely not useful in future) memory page will be copied in disk The frequently/currently used are more important (we might contineu to use them) so we metain them in memory since it is faster to access memory than disk.|

Figure: Example - memory management

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text: Principle Why it matters Separate mechanism from policy Keep mechanisms flexible to support different policies because in different settings, different policies make more sense.  e.g., for memory management: track the frequency and time for: Lest recently used (LRU) vs least frequantly used (LFU) vs random Optimize for the common case Pick a policy that match the device setup (type, CPUs, memory), users' application, workloads requrements. ---

docs.title: Protection boundary: user vs kernel
docs.text:
User - level (unprivileged) kernel - level (privileged) Definition Normal applications run here; cannot directly access hardware OS runs here; can execute privileged instructions and directly access hardware user-kernel transation - attempt when forbidden in user mode will cause a trap, application will be interrupted, hardware enforced transfer to OS, then OS decides: allow/terminate process - set a special bit in CPU = manipulating hardware is permitted; otherwise = forbidden. - OS provide system call interface for applications to invoke: e.g., open(file), send(network socket),mmap(allocate memory). - OS use signals to send notifications to the application ----

Figure: System Call Flow

System call flow explanation: - Issues: - user → kernel → user; the context switching has overhead, not a cheap operation. - application performace (dependent on the ability to use cache) can benifit or suffer based on cache usage. - benifit: when cache contains data/address the applications needs - suffer: otherwise, forcing application to retrieve data from main memory. (OS bring data OS needed into cache, which replaces some application data in the cache ) - Arguments to system call must be written by applications, it can either be passed directly from process to OS, or by specifying their address. Application must save relevant data at well-defined location. - Applications make a system call using specific system call number, OS can determine how many arguments it should retrive from the well defined location, - In synchronous mode, the process waits until the system call completes. Asynchronous modes will be talked in the future.

docs.title: Different types of OS organization (kernel designs)
docs.text: Design What it looks like Pros Cons Monolithic (in the past)  ↓ All the abstractions, services are inside OS, making it very large. - Everything included  - Inlining, compile-time optimizations - Too much code, hard to matain and debug, not customizable/portable / manageable  - Large memory requirement(impact appliataion performance) Modular (common today) basic serivces and APIs  +  loadable modules (Dynamically install new modules) - Maintainable for upgrade  - smaller codebase, less resource intensive (more memory for apps -> better performace) - Have to go through module interface before implementation reduces optimization opportunities (not signaficant)  - module maintenance issues (modules come from disparate code bases with bugs) Microkernel (embedded systems, control systems) Minimal kernel (IPC, address space, threads)  +  Everything else (file systems and disk drivers) will run outside OS kernel at user-level.  It requires lots of interprocess communication (IPC) - Small, lower overhead, better performace  - easy to verify code - Bad portability (often customized to underlying hardware)  - Harder to find common OS components leads to software complexity  - Expensive cost of frequent user/kernel crossing (due to IPC) ---

docs.title: What is a process
docs.text:
a process is an instance of an executing program, sometimes use terms "task" or "job" interchangeably with a "process"

application program → process stored on disk/flash memory/cloud, not executing (static) Once an application is launched loaded into memory and starts executing (active) If the same program (e.g., text editor) is launched more than once multiple processes will be created, they will have different state (e.g. read document_A; type in a empty new document_B ). ---

docs.title: What does a process look like?
Process Address Space and Memory Management
docs.text:
process encapsulates all of the data (code, the data, variables that application need to allocate) of a running application. Every element of the process state has to be uniquely identified by its address.

An operating system abstraction used to encapsulate all of the process state called address space (memory represeatation of a process), defined by a range of addresses from $V_0$ to $V_{max}$. Different types of process state will appear in different regions of the address space.

range Address Space (Virtual address, store process state) property $V_{max}$ stack (e.g., save the state x before jumping to another partion of the code y, after execution of y, restore the state x) Dynamically created state that grows and shrinks as the program executes in a last-in, first-out (LIFO) order. heap (temporary results, read data from files) Dynamically created state; Seems contiguous but might not, portions of the addresses might not allocated $V_0$ text (code), data (the data that is available when process is first initialized) static state ----

Figure: Process address space, process execution example of using stack

The above address space is called virtual address, because they don't have to correspond to actual locations in the physical memory.

OS creates Page table which maintains a mapping between virtual memory addresses and physical memory addresses. By using this mapping, we decouple the complex layout of the data in the virtual address space from the layout of the data in physical memory, to maintain physical memoery management simple.

Note: It is possible for different processes to have the exact same address space range (virtual memory address range), OS will make sure that they point to distinct physical memory locations.

Example of a page table entry |veritual memory| → |physcial memory| |---|:---:|--| |0x03c5||0x0f0f|

whenever the process tries to access x this page table mapping is referenced and the exact physical location where x is will be accessed.

When we do not have enough physical memory to store all the process state, the operating system must maintain information regarding processs address space to dynamically decide which portion of which process's address space will be present in physical memory and which portion will be swapped temporarily to disk, which will be brought in whenever needed.

Figure: Process 1 and Process2 in Physical memory and swap to disk

docs.title: How does OS know what a process is doing?
Process Execution State
docs.text: For an operating system to manage processes, it must have some idea about what a process is "doing". If the operating system stops a process, it must know exactly what it was doing when it was stopped, so the process can resume its execution with the exact same state.

docs.title: Process Control Block
docs.text:
the operating system maintains a process control block (PCB) data structure to maintain all useful information about Process Execution State for every single process.

The PCB is created and initialized when the process is initially created. Certain fields are updated when process state changes; other fields change frequenctly.

Operating system collect all of the data about a process - stored within CPU registers - and save it to the PCB when the process is no longer running.

How to maintain the process state what information change frequency process state process number program counter At any given time, the CPU use it to know where in the a instruction sequence the process currently is every instruction, fast (maintained on CPUs' register) CPU registers other information (e.g., addresses for data, status info) memory limit mapping (virtual-> physical) not too often a list of open file process priority signal mask CPU scheduling info e.g., how much time this particular process had executed in a CPU, how much time it should allocate in the future (depends on process priority) stack pointer The top of the stack (helpful to pop out the top elements of the stack) ... --- Figure: Program Counter

docs.title: Context Switch - How is  Process Control Block (PCB) Used?
docs.text:
context switch: Each time the operating system switches the context of processes.

PCBs are stored in memory. CPU registers holds PCB value of the currently running process (which will ultimately need to be stored in its PCB) If a process is interrupted by the operating system, the operating system save its PCB (including the CPU register value). If a process is resumed, the OS restore its PCB, and update the CPU register with its PCB.

Example: Context Switch of two Processes P1 and P2 |Process P1| Operating system| Process P2| |:---:|:---:|:---:| |running ↓||idle| |interrupted|save PCB of P1, restore PCB of P2|resumed| |idle||running ↓| |running ↓|save PCB of P2, restore PCB of P1|interrupted| |running ↓||idle|

context switch is expensive and we want to limit the frequency of context swtich. - Direct costs: the number of CPU cycles required to load and store PCB to and from memory. - Indirect costs: cold cache and cache misses. Specifically: When a process (e.g., P1) is running on the CPU, its data is stored in the processor cache. Accessing data from cache is much faster than from memory. When the data we need is present in the cache, we called it hot cache (process performance is at its best). When os has to context swtich to another process (e.g., P2) due to higher priority of P2 or timeout of P1, some or all of the data of P1 in the cache will be replaced for new processes P2. The next time when P1 is scheduled, its data is not in the cache (we called it cold cache) and the CPU has to spend many more time to read data from memory (cache misses).

docs.title: Process State
docs.text:
Figure: Process Life Cycle

State Defination When to enter the state new When a process is created ready ready to start executing but isn't currently executing on CPU - When a new process is admitted (OS performs admission control, allocates and initializes the PCB and initial resources for this process.) - When a running process is interrupted and a context switch is performed. - When the I/O operation completes or the event occurs for a waiting process running When the scheduler schedules the process on the CPU waiting When a running process needs to perform some longer I/O operation (e.g., reading data from disk) or wait on an event (e.g., timer, input from a keyboard) terminated When a running process exit: - finish all the operations in the program - encounters some error ---

docs.title: Process Creation
docs.text:
In operating systems, a process can create one or more child processes. The creating process is the parent and the created process is the child of that parent, share a tree-like hierarchy.

Mechanisms for process creation defination fork the operating system will copy the parent PCB into the child PCB. Both parent and child processes will execute at the same point, the instruction immediately after the fork (have same PCB including program counter). exec the operating system will take a PCB (created via fork), but will not leave the values to match the parents' value. Instead OS will replace child image and load a new program. The child's PCB will now point to values that describe this new program. The program counter of the child will now point to the first instruction of the new program. 1. call fork to create the initial process 2. call exec to replace the child's image (created in the fork) with the image of the new program. --- Example: Figure: Process Creation Tree Once the initial boot process is done and OS is loaded, it will create some initial processes. When a user log into a system, a user shell process is created. When user type commands, (e.g., ls, emacs), then new processes get spawned from the shell parent process. OS the parent of all processes --- --- UNIX-based OS init Android zygote ---

docs.title: Role of the CPU Scheduler
docs.text:
Figure: CPU Scheduler For the CPU to start executing a process, the process must be ready first. There might be many processes that are in the ready state waiting in the ready queue.

CPU scheduler is an operating system component that manages how processes use the CPU resources. It determines which ready process will be dispatched to the CPU to start running, and how long that process should run for.

OS must do defination preempt interrupt the executing process, save its current context run scheduling algorithem choose one of the ready processes that should be run next. dispatch dispatch process onto the CPU, and swiched into its context so the process can finally start executing. ----

Since CPU resources are precious, the operating system needs to make sure that CPU time is spent on running processes, not executing OS operatiosn (e.g., scheduling algorithms). Therefore OS should minimize the time for perform avobe OS tasks, so OS must be efficient in the design and implementation in data structure (e.g., waiting processes,priority/history of processes) and algorithms.

docs.title: Length of Process
docs.text:
The longer we run a process, the less frequently we run CPU scheduler, the less CPU time is wasted on running CPU schduler (overhead) instead of running application processes.

Time slice: $T_p$ denotes the time allocated to a process to run on the CPU; $t_{sched}$ denotes the time to run CPU scheduler.

CPU usage efficiency = total processing time / total duration time

Example: If processing time is equal to the CPU schedueler time $T_p = t_{sched}$, then CPU efficiency = 50%, only 50% CPU time spent on useful work.

Figure: CPU effiency 50%

When designing a CPU scheduler, we have to make important design decisions: - approporiate timeslice value - good metrics to choose next process to run

The process will remain in the queue until the device complete the I/O operation, then the process will move to a ready queue. running on CPU but time slice expired create a new process via fork child process executes wait for an interrupt interrupt occcurs --- Figure: A few ways that processes enter the ready queue.

docs.title: Inter Process Communication (IPC)
docs.text:
Many application consist of multiple processes and interract with each other to contribute to a common goal.

Example: Web application. - P1: Web server (front-end) accepts the customer requests. - P2: Database (back-end) stores customer information.

Inter process communication mechanisms (IPCs) - help to transfer data/information between address spaces - maintaining protection and isolation. - provide flexiblility and performance (because different types of interactions between processes exhibit different proerties).

IPC type How it works Pro + Cons - When to use Message Passing IPC Operating system establishes a communication channel, e.g., like a shared buffer. Process interact with each other by - write (send) messages to the channel. - read (recv) messages from the channel. the operating system manages this channel, providing same system calls for write/send and read/recv. overhead: Every single piece of information to be transmitted needs to be copied from user space of the sending process into the channel in the os kernel memory, and back to the address space of the receiving process. Shared Memory IPC The operating system establishes a shared memory channel, and then maps it into the address space of both processes. The processes are then allowed to directly read/write from/to this memory (the same way they can read/write from any memory as if their virtual address space). No overhead from OS: The operating system is completely out of the picture. No well-defined APIs, the usage of the shared memory is more error-prone or developers have to reimplement code. The mapping memory between processes operation is expensive If the setup cost can be amortized across a large number of messages ----

Figure: Message Passing IPC channel between processes. Figure: Shared Memory IPC does not have the extra channel but provides direct communication.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text: Threads visual metaphor worker at a shop  - active entity: executing unit of a process  - works simultaneously with others threads   - requires coordination - sharing of I/O devices, CPUs, memory ----

docs.title: Process vs. Thread
docs.text:
Aspects Process Threads Defination A single-thread process is represented by - its address space (virtual - physical memory mapping) and - its execation context (stack pointer, register, program counter etc). Threads represent multiple independent execution contexts. - shared info: They are within the same virtual address space, which means they share the virtual to physical address mapping, and the code/data/files. - Per-thread info (in a seperate data structure): Threads will potentially execute different instructions and accessing different portions of the address space, operate on different portions of the input etc. This means that each thread will have to have its own different program counter, stack stack, pointer, thread-specific registers. PCB OS represents all the information in a process control block (PCB). More complex PCB: - shared virtual address mapping, code,data - per-thread executaion context. virtual addresss seperate shared execution context ✅ ✅ context switch longer shorter communication mechanisms inter process communication (IPC) (expensive) shared variable (cheap) cache cold hot ----

Figure: Multi-Threads

Figure: Single thread Process vs. Multi Thread Process

docs.title: Benefits of Multithreading
docs.text:
cases reasons in multi-core/multi processor system - Each thread executes same code but for different subset of input (e.g., a matrix)in parallel concurrently on a different processor to speed up - Each thread executes different portions of program for special tasks to set prioirty differently and get performance gain by hot cache why multithreading instead of multiprocess? - lower memory requirement: A multiprocess application requires more memory => more swaps from disk (we have to allocate each process a address space, and a executation context) while a multi-threaded application requires less memory (sharing address space). - lower communication overhead: communicating, passing, synchronizing data among processes (requires inter process communication IPC) is more costly than inter thread communication(shared variables in the same process address space) even on Single CPU or generally when number of threads > the number of CPUs - Hide latency associated with I/O operations: If thread has to wait on some event for some time (t_idle)> two context switche (2*t_ctx_switch), then it makes sense to switch to another thread to perform other operation and switch back. - No memory overhead: Threads shared address space User applications and OS kernel support multiple execution contexts to operate concurrently - OS threads could work on behalf of apps - run OS level services like aemons and device drivers. ---

Figure: Multi-process requires more memory (address space) while multi-threads does not!

Figure: Multi-threading is benificial even on Single CPU

docs.title: overview
docs.text: What we need to support threads Function Meaning thread data structure identify threads, keep track resource usage represent each thread Synchronization Mechanisms - create and manage threads  - allow threads safely coordinate among each other running concurrently in the same address space - don't overwrite each other's inputs or results  - allow one thread to wait on results that should be produced by other threads ---

docs.title: Threads and concurrency
docs.text:
data structure and mechanisms name details thread data structure thread type all the info to represent a thread, including: Thread ID, Program counter, Stack pointer, Register values, Stack, Other thread specific attributes (e.g., for thread management) create a thread parent thread call Fork(proc, args) two arguments: - proc: the procedure that created thread will start executing - args: arguments for the procedure proc. Note that: It is not the UNIX fork. When one thread (parent thread $T_0$) calls fork, a new thread (child thread $T_1$) is created with a new thread data structure (its fields are initialized such that its program counter pointing to the first instructure of the procedure proc and the arguments will be avilable on the stack of the thread). When the thread finishes, store the results of computation in the shared address space and use mechanisms to notify the parent or other threads. terminate a thread parent thread call Join (child thread ID) The parent thread will be blocked until the child completes. Join will return to the parent the result of the child's computation. At that point,child thread exits the system and all the resources allocated for child will be freed. ---

Figure: Thread creation and termination

Figure: Thread creation example: insert element to a shared link list Note: data race: because we do not know which thread will run at which time, we cannot be certain of the ordering of the elements in the shared list. Perhaps the child thread inserts its element before the parent thread, or perhaps the parent thread inserts first.

Figure: data race example: overwriting - insert element to a shared link list If multiple threads running concurrently, the operations are randomly interleaved. Only one element will be ultimately successfully linked to the list; the other one will be lost.

docs.title: Why we need synchronization mechanisms? issues of concurrent execution
docs.text:
Figure: Data Race problem on threads because threads share memory address space

process threads Each process operate within their own address space. The operating system ensures that no valid mapping and access for any address in address space of a process (e.g., P2) to physcial memory (X) which is already mapped to another process (P1) Threads share the same virtual address space and virtual to physical address mappings, which introduces data race problems: one thread can try to read the data while another modifies it, leading to inconsistencies --- #### Synchronization Mechanisms To avoid the issues of concurrent execution Mechanisms Basic Idea --- --- Mutual Exclusion - mutex (like a lock) Whenever accessing shared data/state among threads: only one thread at a time is allowed to access shared data exclusively by acquiring a mutex. The other threads (blocked threads) will be suspended on the lock operation until the mutex owner releases the mutex. Note that there is no guarantee the mutex aquire requests from blocked threads will be granted in order, all of them have chances to get access to mutex. Condition Variable (used with mutex) a thread is waiting on other threads's operation with specific condition before processding. ----

Figure: mutex example: safe insert - insert element to a shared link list

Figure: Condition Variable example: consumer and producer

  • The consumer aquire the mutex, check list is not full, then suspends itself (automatically release the mutex) and waits until the list become full (automatically aquire the mutex).
  • The producer sends signal when the list is full.

docs.title: Readers/Writer Problem using condition variable
docs.text:
At any time, 0 or more readers can access the shared resource; while 0 or 1 writers can access the shared state. The readers and writer cannot access the shared state at the same time.

We can enumerate the cases, condense our two counters into one proxy variable - resource_counter. |cases|state of shared resource encoded by proxy variable resource_counter | |--|---| |if read.counter == 0 and write.counter == 0: can read, can write| free: resource.counter = 0 | |if read.counter > 0 : can read| reading: resource.counter > 0 | |if write.counter == 1 : cannot read, cannot write | writing: resource.counter = -1 (encoding as a negative number) |

Figure: Readers/Writer example implementation:

variables meaning resource_counter a proxy variable representing the state of the shared resourc. Only one thread (both reader/writer) at a time can update/access the resource counter counter_mutex a mutex which always need to be aquired whenever we access to resource_counter read_phase a condition variable signifying that the resource is ready for reading write_phase a condition variable signifying that the resource is ready for writing ---

Readers/Writer with proxy variable implementation - Structure

Benefit: allow more complex sharing senarios: more than one read tBenefithread or only one write thread to be in the critical section at any time. |Steps| Procedures | Details | |--|--|--| | 1| enter critical section block $\approx$ lock | set resource_counter - the shared resource is accessed (using mutex)| | 2| critical section |read/ write shared data (no mutex)| | 3| exit critical section block $\approx$ unlock| reverse resource_counter - free the shared resource and Singal/Broadcast condition variables (using mutex)|

Figure: critical section structure with proxy variable

docs.title: Note: When writing multi-threading
docs.text: What to do Example Write comments about which shared resource/state immediately when defining the mutex/condition variables mutex_type m_f1 // mutex for file 1 always protect access to same shared variable/operation by acquiring the same mutex. use mutex m1 for read and write file 1 Do not forget to use lock and unlock. Make sure that you are signaling or broadcasting on the correct condition. Do not use signal when broadcast are needed. The opposite is actually okay. Remember that the threads execution order is not related to the order of calling signals or broadcasts. If priority are needed, other strategies must be used. Spurious Wake-ups (does not affect correctness but impact performace) Deadlocks

docs.title: Spurious (Unnecessary) Wake-ups
docs.text:
when we wake up threads, but the waken up threads may not be able to proceed.

Figure: Spruious Wake-up

writer readers The writer hold the counter_mutex: sending broadcast and signal readers are waiting on conditiona variable read_phase's queue The writer still holds the counter_mutex: complete the rest of operations before unlock readers are waken up and try to reacquire the mutex, but failed, so they are waiting on the counter_mutex's queue (wait again) -> waste cycles by context switching ---

Solution: |senarios| solutions| |--|--| |when the broadcast/signal are not depended on proxy variable| unlock the mutex before broadcast/signal| |when the broadcast/signal are not depended on proxy variable| no solution since proxy variable should be accessed within mutex lock construct |

docs.title: Deadlocks
docs.text:
occurs when two or more competing threads are waiting on each other to complete, but none of them ever do.

Metaphor: two stubborn workers: each grab a tool and want another tool but do not want to give up the one they have.

Figure: deadlock A cycle in the wait graph is necessary and sufficient for a deadlock to occur. The edges are from the thread waiting on a resource to the thread owning a resource.

Thread T1 Thread T2 aquired mutex for shared resource A aquired mutex for shared resource B aquired mutex for shared resource B, but failed (since it is held by T2) aquired mutex for shared resource A, but failed (since it is held by T1) waiting waiting ---

Solution of deadlock: maintain same order of mutexes for each thread (hard to guarantee though)

Example: |T1| T2| |--|--| |aquired mutex for shared resource A|blocked, waiting| |aquired mutex for shared resource B|waiting| |release all mutexes | start to acquire mutexes A and then B|

Deal with deadlock in real performace critical systems: |solution| meaning |cons| |--|--|--| |prevent deadlocks| Each time to acquire a mutex: check if that operation will cause a cycle in the graph: delay the operation or change code to first release some resource and afterward perform lock request | very expensive| | detect deadlocks and recover| analysis of the wait graph and determine whether any cycles have occurred.| still expensive and sometimes impossible (if input and output are external) due to rollback executation| | doing nothing| hope that the system never have deadlocks, and if we are wrong, just reboot. |

docs.title: Chapter 2: What is a Socket?
docs.text:
Topic Description Core idea A socket is a way for programs to communicate over a network using standard Unix file descriptors. Underlying Unix model In Unix, everything is a file. When Unix programs do I/O, they do it by reading or writing to a file descriptor (an integer associated with an open file). How you create a socket Call socket() to obtain a socket descriptor. How you communicate Use send() / recv() socket calls. Why it matters It gives a standard programming interface for network communication, independent of underlying hardware details. ---

Figure: socket metaphor : post delivery

Figure: TCP

Figure: UDP

docs.text: Item SOCK_STREAM (TCP) SOCK_DGRAM (UDP) Common name Stream socket Datagram socket Connection model Connection-oriented Connectionless by default Communication Channel Yes, reliable two-way connected communication streams. No, don’t have to maintain an open connection Error handling TCP makes sure data arrives sequentially and error-free. No. App may add its own ACK/retry logic if reliability is needed Reliability Reliable delivery Best-effort delivery Ordering Preserves order May arrive out of order Speed/overhead More overhead, generally slower Lower overhead, generally faster Typical use cases ssh, telnet, HTTP/web traffic, chat When a TCP stack is unavailable or when a few dropped packets are acceptable, e.g., tftp (trivial file transfer protocol, a little brother to FTP), dhcpcd (a DHCP client), Real-time multiplayer games, audio/video streaming, DHCP/TFTP-style workflows Key tradeoff Correctness and delivery guarantees Low Latency and throughput with possible packet loss ---

docs.title: Section 2.2: Network Theory
docs.text:
How packets are built:

Topic Description Encapsulation flow App data is wrapped layer-by-layer (e.g., TFTP → UDP → IP → Ethernet) before sending; receiver unwraps in reverse order and finally gets the data. Why layering helps Socket code stays mostly the same even if hardware/topology changes; lower layers abstract details away. Layered Network Model (ISO/OSI 7-layer) Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical. Layered model consistent with Unix (simplified) Application (telnet, ftp, etc) → Host-to-Host Transport (TCP/UDP) → Internet (IP/routing) → Network Access (Ethernet/Wi-Fi). Programmer responsibility Use send() for stream sockets or sendto() for datagrams; kernel/hardware handle most lower-layer header work. ---

Figure: Data Encapsulation a packet is born, the packet is wrapped (“encapsulated”) in a header (rarely a footer) by the first protocol (TFTP protocol), then the whole thing (TFTP header included) is encapsulated again by the next protocol (UDP), then again by the next (IP), then again by the final protocol on the hardware (physical) layer (Ethernet).

Section 3.1: IP Addresses, versions 4 and 6
docs.text: Topic Description Example IPv4 32-bit address, decimal + dot notation 192.0.2.33 its IPv6-compatible form is ::ffff:192.0.2.33. IPv6 128-bit address, hexadecimal + colon notation, created to solve IPv4 exhaustion. shorthand: Leading zeros can be omitted and long runs of zero groups can be compressed with :: (once per address). 2001:0db8:ab00:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000 =2001:db8:ab00:: Loopback address It always means “this machine I’m running on now”. - IPv4 loopback is 127.0.0.1 - IPv6 loopback is ::1. Subnet concept Address = network part + host part, determined by a netmask (outdated). New style (Written as address/the number of network bits (can be arbitrary) in decimal for IPv4: 192.0.2.12/30, for IPv6: 2001:db8::/32 Port numbers 16-bit transport-layer endpoint identifier; same IP can host multiple services by different ports. Metaphor: Think of the IP address as the street address of a hotel, and the port number as the room number. HTTP 80, telnet 23, SMTP 25; ports <1024 are often special, and usually require special OS privileges to use. ---

docs.title: Chapter 5: System Calls or Bust
docs.text: call these functions, the kernel takes over and does all the work for us automagically.

docs.title: Section 5.1: getaddrinfo() — Prepare to launch
docs.text:
Functions: DNS and service name lookups, and fills out the structs we need.

We can use the results to pass to other socket functions to get our network connection established. 

#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <netdb.h>

int getaddrinfo(const char *node,   
                const char *service,  
                const struct addrinfo *hints,
                struct addrinfo **res);

Parameters Description Notes *node (input) - For server: the local bind IP address - For client: the remote server target (hostname e.g. "www.example.com") or IP address) the client wants to connect to - Server setup for listening: - often set it as NULL when setting AI_PASSIVE in hints to bind()to the local host IP address. - Client: If you want to bind to a specific local IP address, drop the AI_PASSIVE in hints and put the IP address. *service (input) Port number (e.g., "80","3490") or service name (e.g., "http", "ftp, "telnet" or "smtp" etc). found in The IANA Port List1 or the /etc/services file on our Unix machine) *hints (input) pointer &hints points to a defined struct addrinfo hints that we’ve already filled out with relevant information. Example: struct addrinfo hints; hints.ai_family = AF_UNSPEC; // IPv4 or IPv6 agnostic hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM; // TCP stream sockets hints.ai_flags = AI_PASSIVE; // fill in my IP for me automatically **res (output) address of a pointer which points to a Linked list res, where each node is struct addrinfo Define pointer struct addrinfo *res and pass the address &res as output parameter int status Return value - 0 : success - non-zero : error error handling: print error using gai_strerror(status). ---

docs.title: Server setup code example
docs.text:
int status;
struct addrinfo hints;
struct addrinfo *res;  // a pointer will point to the results (linked list head)

memset(&hints, 0, sizeof hints); // make sure the struct is empty
// 1. Fill in struct addrinfo hints:
hints.ai_family = AF_UNSPEC;     // don't care IPv4 or IPv6
hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM; // TCP stream sockets
hints.ai_flags = AI_PASSIVE;     // fill in my IP for me

// 2. Error handling: If there’s an error (getaddrinfo() returns non-zero), we can print it out using the function gai_strerror()
if ((status = getaddrinfo(NULL, "3490", &hints, &res)) != 0) {
    fprintf(stderr, "gai error: %s\n", gai_strerror(status));
    exit(1);
}

// 3. If everything works properly: servinfo now poinst to  a linked list of struct addrinfos, each of which contains a struct sockaddr 

// ... do everything until you don't need servinfo anymore ....

freeaddrinfo(res); // 4. Free the linked-list that getaddrinfo() allocated

docs.title: Section 5.2: socket() — Get the File Descriptor
docs.text:
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>

int socket(int domain, int type, int protocol);
Parameters / Return Description Values notes domain (input) Protocol Family (PF) used by the socket. - PF_INET (IPv4) - PF_INET6 (IPv6). People used to hardcode these input values and we can still do that but using results from getaddrinfo() is better. PF_INET thing is close related to AF_INET that they actually have the same value. Use AF_INET in your struct sockaddr_in and PF_INET in your call to socket(). type (input) Communication type. - SOCK_STREAM (TCP) - SOCK_DGRAM (UDP). protocol (input) Specific protocol. - Usually 0 to auto-select the proper protocol for the given type. - Or call getprotobyname() to look up the protocol you want, “tcp” or “udp”. Return value Socket file descriptor - int sockfd on success - -1 on error The global variable errno is set to the error’s value ---

docs.title: code example
docs.text:
int sockfd;
struct addrinfo hints, *res;

// do the lookup
// [pretend we already filled out the "hints" struct]
getaddrinfo("www.example.com", "http", &hints, &res);

// You should do error-checking on getaddrinfo(), and walk the "res" linked list looking for valid entries instead of just assuming the first one is good. See the section on client/server for real examples.

sockfd = socket(res->ai_family, res->ai_socktype, res->ai_protocol); // Feed the values from the results of getaddrinfo() into socket() directly

docs.title: Section 5.3: bind() — What port am I on?
docs.text:
associate that socket with a port on your local machine if you’re going to listen() for incoming connections on a specific port. The port number is used by the kernel to match incoming packets to a certain process’s socket descriptor.

  • Server: usually must call bind() to claim a known local port before listen().
    • Typical server flow: getaddrinfo() → socket() → bind() → listen()
  • Client: usually skip bind() but calls connect() to connect to a remote machine.
    • The kernel’ll check if the socket is unbound, and will bind it to an unused local port automatically if necessary. 
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>

int bind(int sockfd, struct sockaddr *my_addr, int addrlen);
Parameter Description Notes sockfd (input) Socket file descriptor (fd) returned by socket(). This is the local socket you want to attach to a local address/port. my_addr (input) a pointer to a struct sockaddr that contains information about your address, namely, port and IP address Typically use res->ai_addr from res output of getaddrinfo() addrlen (input) Length (bytes) of the address passed in my_addr. Usually res->ai_addrlen Return value Result of bind operation. - 0 on success - -1 on error and sets errno to the error's value. ---

docs.title: Common pitfall and solutions
docs.text:
• Don’t go underboard with port numbers.
    • All ports below 1024 are RESERVED (unless you’re the superuser)!
    • You can have any port number above 1024, up to 65535 (provided they aren’t already being used by another program).
  • If bind() fails with “Address already in use”, add codes: 
    int yes=1;
//char yes='1'; // Solaris people use this

// lose the pesky "Address already in use" error message
setsockopt(listener, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &yes, sizeof yes);

docs.title: code example for server listening:
docs.text:
struct addrinfo hints, *res;
int sockfd;

// load up address structs with getaddrinfo():
memset(&hints, 0, sizeof hints);
hints.ai_family = AF_UNSPEC;  
hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM;
hints.ai_flags = AI_PASSIVE;     

getaddrinfo(NULL, "3490", &hints, &res); // use port ablove 1024 (up to 65535)

// make a socket:
sockfd = socket(res->ai_family, res->ai_socktype, res->ai_protocol);

// bind it to the port we passed in to getaddrinfo():
bind(sockfd, res->ai_addr, res->ai_addrlen);

docs.title: Section 5.4: connect() — client initiate a connection to a remote host.
docs.text:
• Typical client flow: getaddrinfo() → socket() → connect()
  • Usually no bind() needed on the client side; kernel auto-picks a local port.
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>

int connect(int sockfd, struct sockaddr *serv_addr, int addrlen);
Parameter Description Notes sockfd (input) Socket file descriptor returned by socket() serv_addr (input) Pointer to struct sockaddr (containing the destination port and IP address) Usually pass info from getaddrinfo(), i.e., res->ai_addr addrlen (input) Length in bytes of serv_addr. Usually pass info from getaddrinfo(), i.e., res->ai_addrlen. Return value Result of connection attempt. -0 on success - -1 on error and set errno. ---

docs.title: code example for client connect to remote host:
docs.text:
struct addrinfo hints, *res;
int sockfd;

// 1. Load up address structs with getaddrinfo():
memset(&hints, 0, sizeof hints);
hints.ai_family = AF_UNSPEC;
hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM;

getaddrinfo("www.example.com", "3490", &hints, &res);

// 2. make a socket:
sockfd = socket(res->ai_family, res->ai_socktype, res->ai_protocol);

// 3. connect!
connect(sockfd, res->ai_addr, res->ai_addrlen);

docs.title: Section 5.5: listen() — Will somebody please call me?
docs.text:
listen() wait for incoming connections and handle them.

int listen(int sockfd, int backlog);
Parameter Description Notes sockfd (input) Socket file descriptor (fd) returned by socket() system call. backlog (input) the limit about number of connections allowed waiting in the incoming queue until you accept(). Most systems silently limit this number to about 20; you can probably get away with setting it to 5 or 10. Return value Result of listen setup. - 0 on success - -1 on error and sets errno on error. ---

docs.title: server setup flow:
docs.text:
getaddrinfo();
socket();
bind();
listen();
// accept() goes there
- Call bind() before listen() so that the server is running on a specific port and then clients know which port to connect to.

docs.title: Section 5.6: accept() — “Thank you for calling port 3490.”
docs.text:
accept() pulls one pending client connection from the listen queue and returns a new socket descriptor for that connection.

  • The original sockfd (listening socket) keeps listening for new client connections.
  • The returned new_fd is the socket ready to send() / recv() with this specific client.
  • If your server only needs one connection, you can close() the listening socket after accept() to prevent more incoming connections on the same port.
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>

int accept(int sockfd, struct sockaddr *addr, socklen_t *addrlen);
Parameter Description Notes sockfd (input) Listening socket descriptor. addr (output) a pointer to a local struct sockaddr_storage - Define struct sockaddr_storage their_addr; - cast it to (struct sockaddr *) by (struct sockaddr *)&their_addr struct sockaddr_storage is where the information about the incoming connection will go (and with it you can determine which host is calling you from which port). addrlen (input) a local integer variable that should be set to sizeof(struct sockaddr_storage) before its address is passed to accept() addr_size = sizeof their_addr; Return value A new connected socket descriptor. - new_fd >= 0 on success - -1 on error and sets errno. ---

docs.title: code example for server accept():
docs.text:
s#include <string.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <netdb.h>

#define MYPORT "3490"  // the port users will be connecting to
#define BACKLOG 10     // how many pending connections queue holds

int main(void)
{
    struct sockaddr_storage their_addr; // for setting *addr
    socklen_t addr_size; // // for setting *addrlen

    struct addrinfo hints, *res;
    int sockfd, new_fd;

    // !! don't forget your error checking for these calls !!

    // load up address structs with getaddrinfo():
    memset(&hints, 0, sizeof hints);
    hints.ai_family = AF_UNSPEC;  
    hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM;
    hints.ai_flags = AI_PASSIVE;     

    getaddrinfo(NULL, MYPORT, &hints, &res);

    // make a socket, bind it, and listen on it:
    sockfd = socket(res->ai_family, res->ai_socktype,
                                                 res->ai_protocol);
    bind(sockfd, res->ai_addr, res->ai_addrlen);
    listen(sockfd, BACKLOG);

    // Accept an incoming connection:
    addr_size = sizeof their_addr;
    new_fd = accept(sockfd, (struct sockaddr *)&their_addr,
                                                       &addr_size);

    // ready to communicate on socket descriptor new_fd!

docs.title: Section 5.7: send() and recv() — Talk to me!
docs.text:
send() and recv() are for data transfer on stream sockets (TCP) or connected datagram sockets. - For unconnected datagram sockets (UDP), use sendto() / recvfrom() instead.

They are blocking calls: - recv() will block (sleep) until there is some data ready to receive. - send() can also block if the stuff you’re sending is all jammed up somehow, but that’s rarer. 

int send(int sockfd, const void *msg, int len, int flags); 
int recv(int sockfd, void *buf, int len, int flags);
send() Parameter / Return Description Notes sockfd (input) Socket descriptor to send data to. Can be a connected socket returned by socket() or the new_fd returned by accept(). msg (input) a pointer to the data you want to send Example: char *msg = "Your message"; len (input) the length of that data in bytes. Usually strlen(msg) for strings (without \0). flags (input) Send flags. set to 0. Return value Number of bytes actually sent. -1 on error and errno is set to the error number. Note: may send fewer bytes than requested. If the value returned by send() (actually sent) doesn’t match the value in len (intend to send), it’s up to you to send the rest of the string by looping until all bytes are sent. If the packet is small (less than 1K or so) it will probably manage to send the whole thing all in one go. --- recv() Parameter / Return Description Notes sockfd (input) Socket descriptor to receive data from. Usually connected stream socket. buf (output) buffer to read the information into Must have enough allocated memory. len (input) maximum length of the buffer buf. Protects against buffer overflow flags (input) Receive flags. set to 0. Return value Number of bytes actually received into buffer. - -1 on error (errno set) - 0 means remote side closed the connection. ---

docs.title: Section 5.9: close() and shutdown()
docs.text:
After communication is done, use these calls to stop socket I/O.

  • close() closes the socket file descriptor completely.
    • Prevents further reads/writes
    • frees descriptor resource.
  • shutdown() disables communication in certain direction(s). More control than close().
    • but does not free the socket descriptor (need to call close() to fully free it).
close(sockfd);

int shutdown(int sockfd, int how);
Parameters Description Meaning sockfd (input) the socket file descriptor you want to shutdown 0 on success, -1 on error (errno set). how (input) disable direction control - 0: Further receives are disallowed. - 1: Further sends are disallowed. - 2: Further sends and receives are disallowed (similar communication effect to close()). Return value shundown result - 0 on success - -1 on error (errno set) ---

docs.title: Chapter 6: Client-Server Background
docs.text:
Client processes and server processes communicate in request/response style over the network. Note that the client-server pair can speak SOCK_STREAM, SOCK_DGRAM, or anything else (as long as they’re speaking the same thing).

Figure: Client-Server Interaction

aspects Client (multiple) (metaphor: caller) Server (only one) (metaphor: public phone line) Role Initiates connection to a server and requests data/service. listens on a known port, waits for incoming connections and responds to clients. Model Parent process keeps waiting for a connection, accept() it, then fork() a child process to handle each client. Socket - sockfd listening socket (stays open) - new_fd: connected socket for one client Typical stream flow resolve server address getaddrinfo() -> create socket socket() -> call server connect() -> receive reply recv() -> close socket getaddrinfo() -> socket() -> bind() -> listen() -> accept() ---

docs.title: Section 6.1: A Simple Stream Server
docs.text: This demo server accepts TCP connections and sends "Hello, world!" out over the stream connection.

docs.title: minimal server code example
docs.text:
/*
** server.c -- a stream socket server demo
*/

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <netdb.h>
#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>
#include <signal.h>

#define PORT "3490"  // server listens on this TCP port,clients will be connecting to this port

#define BACKLOG 10   // maximum pending connections queue will hold

void sigchld_handler(int s)
{
    (void)s; // quiet unused variable warning

    // waitpid() might overwrite errno, so we save and restore it:
    int saved_errno = errno;

    while(waitpid(-1, NULL, WNOHANG) > 0);

    errno = saved_errno;
}


// get sockaddr, IPv4 or IPv6:
void *get_in_addr(struct sockaddr *sa)
{
    if (sa->sa_family == AF_INET) {
        return &(((struct sockaddr_in*)sa)->sin_addr);
    }

    return &(((struct sockaddr_in6*)sa)->sin6_addr);
}

int main(void)
{
    // listen on sock_fd, new connection on new_fd
    int sockfd, new_fd;
    struct addrinfo hints, *servinfo, *p;
    struct sockaddr_storage their_addr; // connector's address info
    socklen_t sin_size;
    struct sigaction sa;
    int yes=1;
    char s[INET6_ADDRSTRLEN];
    int rv;

    memset(&hints, 0, sizeof hints);
    hints.ai_family = AF_INET;
    hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM;
    hints.ai_flags = AI_PASSIVE; // use my IP

    if ((rv = getaddrinfo(NULL, PORT, &hints, &servinfo)) != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "getaddrinfo: %s\n", gai_strerror(rv));
        return 1;
    }

    // loop through all the results and bind to the first we can
    for(p = servinfo; p != NULL; p = p->ai_next) {
        if ((sockfd = socket(p->ai_family, p->ai_socktype,
                p->ai_protocol)) == -1) {
            perror("server: socket");
            continue;
        }

        if (setsockopt(sockfd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &yes,
                sizeof(int)) == -1) {
            perror("setsockopt");
            exit(1);
        }

        if (bind(sockfd, p->ai_addr, p->ai_addrlen) == -1) {
            close(sockfd);
            perror("server: bind");
            continue;
        }

        break;
    }

    freeaddrinfo(servinfo); // all done with this structure

    if (p == NULL)  {
        fprintf(stderr, "server: failed to bind\n");
        exit(1);
    }

    if (listen(sockfd, BACKLOG) == -1) {
        perror("listen");
        exit(1);
    }

    sa.sa_handler = sigchld_handler; // reap all dead processes
    sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
    sa.sa_flags = SA_RESTART;
    if (sigaction(SIGCHLD, &sa, NULL) == -1) {
        perror("sigaction");
        exit(1);
    }

    printf("server: waiting for connections...\n");

    while(1) {  // main accept() loop
        sin_size = sizeof their_addr;
        new_fd = accept(sockfd, (struct sockaddr *)&their_addr,
            &sin_size);
        if (new_fd == -1) {
            perror("accept");
            continue;
        }

        inet_ntop(their_addr.ss_family,
            get_in_addr((struct sockaddr *)&their_addr),
            s, sizeof s);
        printf("server: got connection from %s\n", s);

        if (!fork()) { // this is the child process
            close(sockfd); // child doesn't need the listener
            if (send(new_fd, "Hello, world!", 13, 0) == -1)
                perror("send");
            close(new_fd);
            exit(0);
        }
        close(new_fd);  // parent doesn't need this
    }

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Section 6.2: A Simple Stream Client
docs.text: This demo client connects to the host we specify on the command line, port 3490, receives the string the server sends.

docs.title: minimal client code example
docs.text:
/*
** client.c -- a stream socket client demo
*/

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <netdb.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>

#include <arpa/inet.h>

#define PORT "3490" // the port client will be connecting to 

#define MAXDATASIZE 100 // max number of bytes we can get at once 

// get sockaddr, IPv4 or IPv6:
void *get_in_addr(struct sockaddr *sa)
{
    if (sa->sa_family == AF_INET) {
        return &(((struct sockaddr_in*)sa)->sin_addr);
    }

    return &(((struct sockaddr_in6*)sa)->sin6_addr);
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    int sockfd, numbytes;  
    char buf[MAXDATASIZE];
    struct addrinfo hints, *servinfo, *p;
    int rv;
    char s[INET6_ADDRSTRLEN];

    if (argc != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr,"usage: client hostname\n");
        exit(1);
    }

    memset(&hints, 0, sizeof hints);
    hints.ai_family = AF_UNSPEC;
    hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM;

    if ((rv = getaddrinfo(argv[1], PORT, &hints, &servinfo)) != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "getaddrinfo: %s\n", gai_strerror(rv));
        return 1;
    }

    // loop through all the results and connect to the first we can
    for(p = servinfo; p != NULL; p = p->ai_next) {
        if ((sockfd = socket(p->ai_family, p->ai_socktype,
                p->ai_protocol)) == -1) {
            perror("client: socket");
            continue;
        }

        inet_ntop(p->ai_family,
            get_in_addr((struct sockaddr *)p->ai_addr),
            s, sizeof s);
        printf("client: attempting connection to %s\n", s);

        if (connect(sockfd, p->ai_addr, p->ai_addrlen) == -1) {
            perror("client: connect");
            close(sockfd);
            continue;
        }

        break;
    }

    if (p == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "client: failed to connect\n");
        return 2;
    }

    inet_ntop(p->ai_family,
            get_in_addr((struct sockaddr *)p->ai_addr),
            s, sizeof s);
    printf("client: connected to %s\n", s);

    freeaddrinfo(servinfo); // all done with this structure

    if ((numbytes = recv(sockfd, buf, MAXDATASIZE-1, 0)) == -1) {
        perror("recv");
        exit(1);
    }

    buf[numbytes] = '\0';

    printf("client: received '%s'\n",buf);

    close(sockfd);

    return 0;
}

docs.text: Concept Meaning Indentification Used For / Scope Fungible Asset Interchangeable asset with identical value but ≠ identical asset identifiers Stocks, bonds, ETFs, gold, Bitcoin, paper currency in any country,  diamonds without engraved serial number by GIA (with risks that it is not properly appraised for clarity or carats or might be actually man-made or fake.) Infungible Asset Unique or non-interchangeable items. no identifiers, use deed or property record, often filed at the local level Real estate, art, jewelry (Diamonds with engraved serial number by GIA), collectibles. ---

docs.title: Time Zones, Trading Days, and 24/7 Trading
docs.text:
Financial data across markets occur in different time zones and trading hours, so even simple comparisons (like daily prices or returns) can be misleading if timestamps are not aligned. Always verify when data was recorded before calculating correlations, returns, or building strategies.

Concept Meaning Example or Implication Asynchronous data A single day’s close price varies by geographic market and time zone. Lagos (GMT+1) vs. Sydney (GMT+10) = 9-hour difference between official closes. → adjust timestamps to a common reference (e.g., GMT). Timestamp alignment Before analyzing or correlating data, adjust local timestamps to a common reference (e.g., GMT). Note: For statistical analysis, e.g., correlation, use both markets’ latest available data (e.g., close price). avoid reversing cause and effect Do not use information not yet known at the time of trading, which creates a false predictive signal. If you were to build a trading strategy using closing price correlation and decided to buy XX, it would have to be for the following trading day. OTC market issue OTC (Over-The-Counter) instruments trade across cities without a central exchange. There is no single “official closing price” for the day and each trading center (Tokyo, London, New York) has its own “closing quote.” The quality of your data vendor become critical. (Are they providing the time zone, market, currency, etc.?) 24/7 trading assets Some assets (e.g., Bitcoin) trade continuously. there’s no daily closing. data vendors pick an consistent daily cutoff time to define a “daily close.” (e.g., 00:00 GMT) for daily aggregation.

docs.title: 💡 Takeaways
docs.text:
• Always check timestamp, time zone, and trading-day definitions before comparing markets.
  • Even daily or closing-price data require time alignment to avoid misleading results.
  • Don’t mix data from different local days — otherwise, you may introduce look-ahead bias.
  • OTC and crypto markets complicate this further because they lack a universal close time.
  • Consistency is more important than local convention — pick one time reference (e.g., GMT) and apply it to all data.

docs.title: Covariance vs. Correlation
docs.text: Metric Meaning Formula Range How to Interpret Covariance Measures the amount of movement the two variables exhibit together.  Downside: value changes when variable scales change $ \mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) = \ E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])] $ (−∞, +∞) • Positive sign: move in the same direction• Negative sign: move in opposite directions• 0: linearly uncorrelated• Higher absolute value: stronger positive or negative relationship Correlation Measures the co-movement of two variables but removes the scale issue $ \mathrm{Corr}(X, Y) = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)\,\mathrm{Var}(Y)}} $ −1 to +1 • > 0: positively correlated. 1: Perfect positively correlated • < 0: negatively correlated -1: Perfect negatively correlated • 0: linearly uncorrelated ---

docs.title: Collinear Variables
docs.text: Concept Meaning (Notebook Summary) How to Detect / How to Read Collinearity When two variables move together in systematic ways; they are correlated Check their correlation value: if they move together → correlated (collinear) Multicollinearity When more than two variables are correlated Use the correlation matrix to see all pairwise correlations among many variables covariance matrix a matrix that contains all pairwise covariances from all variables. The diagonal elements of the covariance matrix are also the variance of the variables Correlation Matrix A matrix showing the correlation between every pair of variables Upper-right triangle shows correlations; lower-left triangle provides the same correlation information as the upper right triangle; diagonal is 1 (variable correlated with itself)

docs.title: Impact of Multicollinearity in Regression Model
docs.text: If independent variables are highly correlated | Effect of Multicollinearity | Indication | Why It Matters | |-----------------------------|--------------------------------|----------------| | Large variances & standard errors and covariances of the coefficients | Regression cannot distinguish which correlated X variable drives Y | Coefficients become unstable and noisy | | Wide confidence intervals** for the coefficient estimates | Estimates become less precise | Hard to trust the coefficient values | | High p-values (less significant) | Even important variables may appear insignificant | May drop variables incorrectly | | R² and Adjusted R² may still be high | The model as a whole still explains Y well | Good overall prediction even if individual betas are unreliable | | Hard to isolate each variable’s individual effect | Correlated variables “share credit” | Interpretation becomes difficult | | Model may still forecast well | If future Xs of test data have the same correlation patterns as training data | Good for prediction, bad for explanation |

docs.title: Methods to Address Multicollinearity
docs.text: Method What to do Notes Method 1: Drop Highly Correlated Variables Identify independent variables with high correlation (usually 0.8–0.9), then drop one and re-run the regression model to see if the model improves • Only considers pairwise relationships (two variables at a time) • Cannot detect multicollinearity involving >2 variables • using correlation alone cannot find this issue. Method 2: to determine if any of the independent variables can be explained by the other independent variables Treat one independent variable as dependent as a dependent variable and run a regression with the rest of the independent variables. Use variance inflation factor (VIF) to determine if an independent variable has a multicollinearity issue  $VIF = \frac{1}{(1 − R²)} $ • VIF starts at 1 and has no upper limit • When R² = 0 → VIF = 1 → no multicollinearity • higher R² → Higher VIF = more multicollinearity • VIF 1–5 → no severe multicollinearity • VIF > 5 → severe multicollinearity Method 3: Use principal components from Principal Component Analysis (PCA) 1. Use PCA to create new variables (principal components) that are independent (uncorrelated/ orthogonal), and select the first few components to replace the original correlated variable.  2. Choose the top k principal components explain most (e.g.about 95%+) of the total variance.  3. For the k principal components, choose the original variable with the highest absolute value of the coefficient in the linear combination as a proxy of that principal component or   look for a financial theme from the loadings of a principal component and select original variables related to the theme.  4. rerun to the revised model with fewer independent variables to see the difference. • Each principal components is a linear function of the original variables •  PCs preserve as much information (variation) as possible.  • PCA also ranks each principal component's ability to explain the dataset variation. The first principal component has the highest ability to explain the variation of the dataset.   • It allows reducing many variables to a smaller set (dimension reduction)  •  Note: By selecting the top variables from PCA for data analysis, there is a trade-off between reducing multicollinearity and losing data explaining accuracy, which will depend on a researcher's experience in data analysis. ---

docs.title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
docs.text: Baic idea: PCA rotates the original coordinate system into a new one whose axes (principal components) capture the most variance and are uncorrelated, allowing us to reduce dimensionality and remove multicollinearity.

docs.title: Derivation of Principal Components
docs.text: Step What You Do Explanation / Formula 1. Standardize the Dataset Convert each variable to standardized form.  • Ensures all variables have the same scale  Mean = 0 and variance = 1 $ \text{Standardized Variable} = \frac{\text{Original Variable} - \text{Mean}}{\text{Standard Deviation}} $ 2. Calculate the Covariance Matrix of the Standardized Variables Compute pairwise covariances between all standardized variables $\text{Covariance} = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{N} $   Diagonal elements = variances of the variables  $Var(X) = E[(X - E(X))^2]= Cov(X,X)$ 3. Calculate Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues from the covariance matrix Use linear algebra to obtain eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the covariance matrix.  Note: most software doesn't readily provide eigenvalues. They instead provide a proportion of the total variance explained by the principal component. This proportion is calculated from the eigenvalue of the principal component. • Eigenvectors are the direction of the principal components  • Eigenvalues show how much variance each principal component explains  • The component with the largest eigenvalue = PC₁  • The second largest = PC₂, etc. 4. Transform the Original Variables into Principal Components generate PCs by linear combination of eigenvectors, i.e., Multiply the standardized data by the transformation matrix $PC = W^TX$ Transformation matrix  (stacking eigenvectors, columns = eigenvectors, e.g., $(a_1, a_2)$ for PC₁):  $W = \begin{pmatrix} a_1 & b_1 \ a_2 & b_2 \end{pmatrix}$   $PC_1 = a_1 Var_1 + a_2 Var_2$  $PC_2 = b_1 Var_1 + b_2 Var_2$ ---

Step Meaning / Examples Key Actions 1.1 Identify potential factors that impact the stock price and collect data e.g., sales, whole stock market movement trends Research economic, market, and company-specific factors, Collect relevant data 1.2 Quantify relationships between stock price and selected factors by building a model e.g., linear regression analysis select models 1.3 Predict future stock price e.g., simulate how much the stock price would change given a 0.5% increase, 1% increase, and 2% increase in revenue. Convert selected factors into measurable numerical variables and convert the variables into comparable returns or ratios. , e.g., quarterly excess returns and quarterly sales growth 2. Decide Y (dependent) and X (independent) variables • Y: An endogenous variable, also called a dependent variable: whose value is determined by the model. • X: An exogenous variable, also called an independent variable: whose value is determined outside of the model or is given to us. 3. Check relationship between Y (dependent) and X (independent) variables use scatter plot; use Pearson Correlation For scatter plot: • If draw a straight line where most of the points will be around the line (oval shape) => linear relationship • if the straight line drawn is either a horizontal line or a vertical line => The exogenous variable is independent of the endogenous variable => we should drop this exogenous variable from the model. • If find extreme points that are well-separated from the other points., e.g., 1. An outlier is a point that doesn't follow the general trend of the other points. 2. A leverage point has extreme value for exogenous variables. Both types may or may not impact the estimated result of the regression model. =>Try to run one model with them and another model without them. => Then, compare the two model results to see if these extreme points are crucial to the final model result. For Pearson Correlation [-1, 1]: • If the value of two variables tends to move in the same direction, the correlation is positive. A correlation towards $1$ means the two variables have a perfectly positive linear relationship, while towards 0 means less and less linear relationship. • If the two variables tend to move in opposite directions, the number is negative. 4. build the regression model. 5. Assess the Model fit ---

Note: * Why excess return? * Finance theory tells us a stock excess return is a better variable to analyze than the actual price. The excess return is the actual return minus risk-free interest rate (usually Treasury Bill Rates),to explain the part of the return that comes from taking additional risk than deposit it in banks with zero risk. * Why quarterly data? * Because daily data is noisy. Quarterly data matches how real economic factors move (Many important financial things only change every 3 months, such as: company earnings, interest rate policy, GDP growth, inflation trends, industry performance).

docs.title: OLS Regression
docs.text: Concept Formula / Definition Meaning Simple OLS model $ Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \varepsilon $ Estimate Y using one factor X Multiple OLS model $Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \cdots + \epsilon $ Estimate Y using several factors.  $\beta$ are called parameters or coefficients. Once the values of the parameters are obtained from the OLS calculation, we call these values estimates. ---

docs.title: OLS Assumptions
docs.text:
OLS Assumption Meaning / Mathematical Form What Violation Causes How to Detect How to Fix (Methods) 1. Linearity (correct functional form) Relationship between X and Y is linear: $ Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \dots + \beta_k X_k + \epsilon $ Model misspecification → unreliable coefficients, standard errors and biased estimates • Residual plots show curvature • Likelihood ratio (LR) test Get the form correct by trial and error • Add polynomial terms • Transform variables (e.g., log, sqrt, Box-Cox) • Use nonlinear models 2.No Multicollinearity X variables are not correlated themselves: $ X_1 \neq c_1 X_2 + ... $ coefficients and standard errors of affected variables are not reliable • High correlation values between X variables • High Variance Inflation Factors(VIF) > 5 • Drop variables • principal component analysis (PCA) • factor analysis 3. Independence of Errors Errors are independent: $ \text{Cov}(\epsilon_i, \epsilon_j) = 0 \; (i \neq j) $ Autocorrelation (occur for time series data) → unreliable standard errors • Durbin-Watson test (specifically for the autocorrelation of the first -order, i.e., t-1) • Breusch-Godfrey test (generally, beyond first-order) • Investigate omitted variables • Generalised idfference equation(Cochrane-Orchutt or AR(1) methods) • Use time-series models 4. Normality of Errors Errors normally distributed: $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ if n is small, unreliable standard errors • histogram (not bell shape) • QQ-plot(deviates from the line) • Shapiro-Wilk test • Komologorov-Smirnov test • Anderson-Darling test • change functional form 5. Zero Mean of Errors (omiited variables) $E[\epsilon] = 0$ The error term accounts for the variation in the dependent variable that the independent variables do not explain. A non-zero average error indicates that our model systematically underpredicts the observed values and we should add that information to the regression model. Model can only be used for predictive purpose (cannot infer causation) Residual mean not near zero • using instrumental variables 6. Homoscedasticity (Constant Variance) The variances of error terms are constant: $\text{Var}(Y|X) = \text{Var}(\epsilon|X) = \sigma^2$ The error terms are not constant (Heteroscedasticity) → coefficients remain unbiased, but standard errors are unreliable • Residual plot shows one or more fan/ cone/ megaphone shapes (Residuals are either concentrated and spread out for different values of X variable), but sometimes difficult to detect tests: (same rule: p-value < 0.05) • White test (preferred, any form of heteroscedasticity) • Breusch-Pagan(BP) test (only linear) • Weighted Least Squares (WLS) • White's standard errors ---

Footnote * Residuals are the differences between measured values of the dependent variables and predicted values of dependent variables from the OLS regression model. * Error Term Distribution and Variance Structure (from OLS Assumptions 4, 5, 6): > > Under the OLS assumptions of zero-mean errors, homoscedasticity, and independence of errors, > the error terms are IID (independent and identically distributed): > > $$ e \sim N(0,\sigma^2) $$ > > The regression mean function can be written as: > > $$ E(Y \mid X) = \beta X $$ > > And the conditional variance of error term $e$ (equivalently, of $Y$ is constant): > > $$ \operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X) = \operatorname{Var}(e \mid X) = \sigma^2 $$ > > Because we have multiple observations, the variance of the error variance is a covariance matrix. > * Independence ⇒ all off-diagonal elements are zero. > * Homoscedasticity ⇒ all diagonal elements equal the same constant variance. > > $$ > \operatorname{Var}(e) = > \begin{pmatrix} > \sigma^2 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \ > 0 & \sigma^2 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \ > 0 & 0 & \sigma^2 & \cdots & 0 \ > \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \ > 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & \sigma^2 > \end{pmatrix} > $$
